topic: XGBoost-style column subsampling and L1 shrinkage transferred to neural BoW
guidance: Test this idea: Vocabulary-column dropout plus row-wise L1 on the embedding lowers error more than standard hidden dropout plus L2. Most of the gain comes from column subsampling. (expected: Column subsampling at rate 0.2-0.4 with group-L1 at 1e-6 to 1e-5 gives val_top1_err of about 12.0-12.6, versus 13.3 for the baseline and about 12.8 for tuned hidden dropout plus L2 alone.). Experiment plan: Augmentation edit: a per-batch mask that drops a fraction p in {0.1, 0.2, 0.4} of vocabulary columns before the embedding sum. Regularization edit: group-L1 (sum of L2 norms of embedding rows) with coefficient in {0, 1e-6, 1e-5, 1e-4}. Schedule edit: lr 1e-3 with EMA decay 0.999 for 16 epochs, versus the default. Ablate each component separately, then combine. Compare against hidden dropout plus weight decay tuned with the same 12-trial budget. Use 3 seeds.
lit_context:
Chosen idea: XGBoost-style column subsampling and L1 shrinkage transferred to neural BoW. XGBoost regularizes sparse inputs with per-tree column subsampling, L1/L2 penalties on leaf weights, and shrinkage. This idea transfers each mechanism to the BoW MLP. Column subsampling becomes word-level input dropout: random vocabulary columns are zeroed per batch, with a fresh vocabulary mask per step. Leaf L1 becomes an L1 penalty on embedding rows, which sparsifies the word features. Shrinkage becomes a low-lr, many-epoch schedule with Polyak/EMA weight averaging.
Gap it attacks: Gap 2 (boosting regularizers vs dropout and weight decay on 10k-label text)
Supporting papers:
- [arXiv:1603.02754] XGBoost: A Scalable Tree Boosting System: Regularized boosting objective (L1/L2 on leaf weights, shrinkage, subsampling) with sparsity-aware splits suited to high-dimensional sparse inputs like BoW.

steer.interest: I want to know which cheap regularizers actually help a small bag-of-embeddings text classifier when labels are scarce, and why, rather than collecting another leaderboard point.
hunches: Word dropout helps mostly because it stops the model from leaning on a few topic-specific tokens, not because it acts like generic noise.
Part of any reported gain is early stopping in disguise: a regularized model simply peaks later within the same epoch budget.
avoid: Pure hyperparameter sweeps with no mechanism behind them
steer.contribution: A mechanism claim with a matched control; a clean negative result is welcome.
known: A logistic-regression baseline reaches about 13.3% error on this split
